core_summary: This chapter investigates how animals and plants respond to external stimuli through coordinated regulatory systems. In animals, it details the central and peripheral nervous systems, structural features of neurons, synaptic chemical signal transmission, reflex arcs, and brain anatomy (forebrain, midbrain, hindbrain). In plants, it distinguishes directional tropic movements from non-directional nastic movements and explains plant hormone action. Finally, it outlines human endocrine glands and hormonal feedback control mechanisms.
key_concepts: Nervous coordination in animals via electrical nerve impulses along specialised nerve cells (neurons)
Neuron structural components: Dendrites (signal acquisition), Axon (electrical transmission), and Synapse (chemical neurotransmitter release)
Reflex action as rapid, involuntary emergency responses mediated directly by spinal cord reflex arcs
Central Nervous System (CNS) comprising Brain and Spinal Cord, protected by cranium, vertebral column, and cerebrospinal fluid

Functional regions of the human brain: Forebrain (cerebrum for thinking, memory, voluntary actions), Midbrain and Hindbrain (cerebellum for posture/balance, medulla for involuntary cardiac/respiratory/vascular control, pons)
Plant movements: Nastic (non-directional growth-independent movements like Mimosa leaf drooping) versus Tropic (directional growth movements: phototropism, geotropism, hydrotropism, chemotropism)
Plant hormones (phytohormones): Auxins (cell elongation), Gibberellins (stem growth), Cytokinins (cell division), and Abscisic acid (growth inhibitor, leaf wilting)

Animal Endocrine System secreting chemical messengers (hormones) into bloodstream: Pituitary (growth hormone), Thyroid (thyroxin), Pancreas (insulin), Adrenals (adrenaline), Testes (testosterone), Ovaries (oestrogen)
Hormonal feedback mechanisms regulating hormonal concentration and secretion timing

key_terms.definition: The structural and functional unit of the nervous system specialised for receiving and conducting electrical impulses.
The microscopic gap between the axon terminal of one neuron and the dendrite of the next, across which chemical signals diffuse.
The neural pathway formed by sensory neuron, spinal cord interneuron, and motor neuron that executes a reflex action.
The primary control center of the body consisting of the brain and spinal cord.
Network of cranial nerves arising from the brain and spinal nerves arising from the spinal cord.
Part of the hindbrain responsible for precision of voluntary movements and maintaining body posture and equilibrium.
Part of the hindbrain controlling vital involuntary functions such as heart rate, blood pressure, salivation, and vomiting.
The directional growth movement of a plant part in response to an external environmental stimulus.
Chemical regulators synthesized naturally in plants that control growth, development, and environmental responses.
A ductless gland that secretes hormones directly into the bloodstream to reach target organs.
Emergency hormone secreted by adrenal glands that increases heart rate, blood pressure, and breathing during fight-or-flight stress.
Hormone produced by the pancreas that regulates and lowers blood glucose levels.
A regulatory biological control loop that adjusts the timing and quantity of hormone release based on circulating body levels.

key_takeaways: Nervous signals travel rapidly as electrical impulses along axons but convert to chemical signals across synaptic gaps.
Reflex arcs bypass conscious brain processing to provide instantaneous protective reactions to danger.
Plant shoots show positive phototropism and negative geotropism due to shade-side auxin accumulation causing differential cell elongation.
Iodine in diet is essential for thyroid synthesis of thyroxin, which regulates carbohydrate, protein, and fat metabolism; deficiency causes goitre.
Diabetes mellitus occurs due to insufficient pancreatic insulin production, leading to elevated blood sugar levels.
